messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David Mercer, a 68-year-old school counselor, came to treatment after more than a year of trying to manage on his own following an assault that took place on his walk back to the parking garage after an evening district meeting. A man who smelled strongly of alcohol stepped out from behind a concrete pillar, grabbed him, and shoved him hard against the wall. What stayed with David was not a smooth narrative of the attack but a set of sharp, frozen images: the glint of the man’s belt buckle under the garage light, the blur of a hand at his collar, the concrete close to his face, the sour alcohol on the man’s breath. He was taken to the hospital afterward for evaluation, and the sting of antiseptic on his skin and in the room became bound up with the same fear. When he speaks about it now, he does not tell the story straight through. He describes “pictures,” a few moments that stand alone, and says that remembering them brings back the same terror he felt at the time, as if no time has passed at all.

In the months after the assault, these fragments began to break through without warning. At school, walking past the nurse’s office after surfaces had been cleaned, he would catch that hospital-antiseptic smell and suddenly be back in one of those snapshots, his body seized by the original terror before he had time to think. If a parent arrived for a conference carrying the faint smell of alcohol from a lunch drink or the night before, a piece of the memory would flash up and vanish just as quickly, leaving him shaken and embarrassed. What surprised him most was that emotional closeness could work the same way. When his wife sat beside him and tried to ask what he had been feeling since the attack, or when a distressed student leaned in with trust and vulnerability, something about the intimacy itself seemed to open the door to those same abrupt fragments. The memory did not come as a full account he could sort through. It came as isolated pictures and the immediate conviction that he was in danger again.

David responded by trying not to be fully present when the memories broke through. He learned to blank out deliberately, to go distant in his own words, as if leaving his body could get him through the wave of terror that arrived with the images. He also began avoiding people more generally, keeping his office door partly closed when he could, shortening conversations in the hallway, and limiting casual contact with colleagues. At home he became especially guarded with his wife. Because moments of emotional closeness could stir up those vivid fragments, he began to avoid intimacy too, steering conversations toward practical matters, going to bed later than she did, and pulling back whenever she tried to reach him emotionally. From his point of view this made sense: if remembering meant reliving, then distance and numbing were the safest options available.

Over time, though, these habits seemed to make the world feel narrower and more loaded. The more David avoided people and retreated from closeness, the more charged ordinary encounters became when he could not avoid them. In his work as a counselor, the job itself put him directly in situations he had started to fear: sitting in close emotional contact with students, listening to family crises, being present with tears and trust. He found himself bracing before appointments, and the very fact of someone turning toward him with feeling could act as a trigger. He would catch a whiff of disinfectant in the counseling office after the custodian had cleaned, or alcohol on a parent at dismissal, and those isolated, terrifying images would hit even harder against the blankness he had been trying to maintain. His efforts to leave his body and keep others at a distance seemed to leave him less able to absorb what was happening around him, so the smells and moments of closeness stood out with more force, immediately tied to the assault.

His marriage has been strained by this withdrawal. His wife has told him she feels she is living beside him rather than with him, and David does not disagree, though he feels ashamed rather than angry. He is frightened by how quickly a smell or a moment of connection can make the memory appear in pieces and disappear again, leaving him disoriented. What finally brought him in was an incident at school when a student, crying over a family emergency, reached for a box of tissues just after the office had been cleaned. The antiseptic smell rose, David felt the familiar snapshots slam into him, and he went mentally blank in the middle of the session. He is seeking help now because he is afraid that if he cannot stop retreating from people, he will lose both the work that has defined him and the closeness of his marriage; at the same time, he still hopes there might be a way to remember what happened without being overtaken by the same terror every time.
